entry.evidence: Yet how climate change affects MHWs over LMEs remains unknown because such LMEs are confined to the coast where low-resolution climate models are known to [...]

steps.action: Takes from satellite and field SST studies that historical MHWs have become longer, more frequent and more extensive, mainly from mean warming.
steps.quote: MHWs have become longer lasting, more frequent and more extensive

steps.action: Takes from prior regional and global model studies that MHWs intensify under warming when defined against a fixed historical (mean warming-inclusive) threshold.
steps.quote: the majority of ocean areas is projected to experience almost permanent heatwaves

steps.action: Cites model comparisons showing that 0.1° ocean grids and ~10 km regional models reproduce observed MHWs better than coarse models.
steps.quote: the simulations at 0.1° generally yield the realistic results in reproducing the frequency and duration of global MHWs

steps.action: Poses the question of how MHWs over coastal LMEs change under warming once the built-in increase from mean warming is removed, and with eddies resolved.
steps.quote: obscuring changes in characters that are specific to LMEs

steps.action: Uses an existing 1850-2100 eddy-resolving CESM1.3 simulation (0.1° ocean, 0.25° atmosphere; historical forcing then RCP 8.5) built in the authors' consortium's earlier work, with CESM-LR and 20 CMIP5 models for comparison.
steps.quote: high-resolution CESM1.3 is used for simulation from 1850 to 2100

steps.action: Computes MHW frequency and mean intensity from OISST v2.1 and GMPE daily SST (1982-2011) using the Hobday 90th-percentile, five-day definition.
steps.quote: is used to calculate the MHW index globally in the study

steps.action: Compares historical MHW frequency and intensity from CESM-HR, CESM-LR and CMIP5 with the observations (maps, zonal means, LME groups, P<0.05), finding smaller biases in CESM-HR but overestimated WBC intensity.
steps.quote: biases of MHW frequency in CESM-HR, CESM-LR and CMIP5 relative to OISST are −0.31, −0.55 and −0.60

steps.action: Checks the model evaluation against a second observational product (GMPE) and repeats it over the overlapping 1982-2011 period instead of 1975-2004.
steps.quote: was also used in model evaluation, yielding similar results

steps.action: Explains the CESM-HR excess of WBC intensity partly by the coarser 0.25° satellite SST underestimating eddy-scale variability, rather than by model error alone.
steps.quote: might lead to underestimation of SST variability at mesoscale-eddy-resolving resolution

steps.action: Retains CESM-HR as more skilful than the coarse models for MHW frequency and intensity, as a basis for the projections.
steps.quote: CESM-HR is more skilful in reproducing the frequency and mean intensity of MHWs

steps.action: Designs the projection analysis with two thresholds: the historical 1975-2004 90th percentile (mean warming-inclusive) and the 2071-2100 90th percentile (future threshold).
steps.quote: to isolate the effect of mean background warming and higher statistical moments of SST on MHWs

steps.action: Projects 2071-2100 MHWs with the mean warming-inclusive threshold in CESM-HR: about 287 more annual MHW days and +1.2 °C mean intensity, near-permanent MHWs in the tropics.
steps.quote: CESM-HR projects strong increases in annual MHW days

steps.action: Estimates the share of the projected change due to mean warming alone with a pseudo scenario: historical daily SST plus the 30-year mean SST difference (94% or more).
steps.quote: explains 94% or more of the simulated changes

steps.action: Projects MHWs with the future threshold in CESM-HR: +2.8 annual days and +0.2 °C mean intensity, with more uniform increases across hemispheres.
steps.quote: much smaller increases in annual MHW days and average MHW intensity are projected

steps.action: Compares the future-threshold result with coarse-resolution studies using similar methods for the northeast Pacific and North Atlantic, which found comparably small changes.
steps.quote: yields comparably small changes in the annual MHW days over the northeast Pacific Blob

steps.action: Repeats the two-threshold projection with CESM-LR and the CMIP5 ensemble; the threshold dependence holds, but the coarse models lack the distinct WBC changes.
steps.page: §4 ¶5; Extended Data Fig. 4 (p. 13); Extended Data Fig. 5 (p. 14)
steps.quote: Analysis using CESM-LR and the CMIP5 multimodel ensemble in general supports the findings

steps.action: Explains the meridional dipole of intensity change in WBC regions by changes in detrended SST variance, probably from frontal shifts.
steps.quote: The dipole feature can be explained by changes in the detrended SST variance

steps.action: Computes future-threshold and inclusive-threshold MHW days and intensity per LME for 1975-2004 and 2071-2100: 98% of LMEs gain MHW days and 93% gain intensity under the future threshold.
steps.quote: A total of 98% (except one) of LMEs show more MHWs days

steps.action: Relates LME-mean MHW intensity to SST standard deviation across LMEs in both periods (R = 0.97 and 0.96) to attribute the intensity increase to variance.
steps.quote: a statistically significant correlation (P < 0.05) between MHW intensity and SST variance

steps.action: Attributes the increased SST variance over LMEs, in part, to published projected changes in ENSO, north tropical Atlantic variability, the Indian Ocean Dipole and North Pacific air-sea coupling.
steps.quote: at least in part attributable to strengthened El Niño/Southern Oscillation variability

steps.action: Compares future with historical LME intensities (r = 0.9 under the future threshold vs 0.6 under the inclusive threshold) and top-15-catch LMEs (category I) with the others (category II).
steps.quote: there is a significant correlation of 0.9 (P < 0.05) between the future and historical mean intensities over all LMEs

steps.action: Restricts the interpretation: the future-threshold increase applies only if species adapt fully to mean warming, so it is a lower bound on impact.
steps.quote: can be considered the ‘most optimistic’ scenario for establishing the lower bound

steps.action: Keeps the claim that MHW intensity and annual days increase over most LMEs even under the future threshold, posing a serious threat.
steps.quote: We find increased intensity and annual days of MHWs over the majority of the LMEs

tree.answer: Future marine heatwaves over coastal large marine ecosystems, beyond the effect of mean warming
Historical MHWs observed by satellite; future MHWs not observable, so simulated
Estimate future MHW days and intensity per LME with an eddy-resolving model
No rival hypotheses; two threshold definitions bracket adaptation scenarios, and low- vs high-resolution models are compared
Thresholds give very different magnitudes; HR vs LR differ in WBC behaviour, but no crucial test between rivals
Conditions set in a single model run (historical forcing then RCP 8.5)
Model evaluation holds against two observational products and an alternative period; projections broadly supported by CESM-LR and CMIP5
Kept: increases over most LMEs even under the future threshold

end.claim: Under RCP 8.5 in the eddy-resolving CESM-HR, MHW intensity and annual days increase over most LMEs by 2071-2100 even with a future threshold above mean warming (about +2.8 days and +0.2 °C on average; 98% and 93% of LMEs), a lower bound on threat if organisms adapt fully to mean warming.

decisive_move.sentence: Applying the future (2071-2100) 90th-percentile threshold to the eddy-resolving CESM-HR output removes the built-in mean-warming increase; without it the LME-specific claim of residual increases would not exist.

gates.evidence: The simulation pre-existed (inherited, ref. 28) and was not acquired to test a stated hypothesis. The model's historical skill was tested against OISST and GMPE and could have failed (§3). The headline future claim is a projection with no test it could fail; only consistency with CESM-LR, CMIP5 and prior coarse studies is shown (§4 ¶4-5). No pre-specified hypotheses, thresholds or analyses are reported.

imports.item: Large marine ecosystem (LME) concept and boundaries, with fisheries-catch categories
Organism adaptation to mean warming, used to interpret the future threshold as a full-adaptation scenario
Ecological impact evidence (coral bleaching, seagrass decline, fish spawning and distribution shifts, barnacle mortality)

novelty_claims.quote: Yet how climate change affects MHWs over LMEs remains unknown
Better resolution of ocean mesoscale eddies enables simulation of more realistic MHWs than low-resolution models.

limits: The headline projection rests on a single realization of one high-resolution model under one scenario (RCP 8.5). The paper gives no uncertainty range or internal-variability spread for the per-LME changes, so 'estimate_with_resolution' is generous: the resolution is spatial (0.1° ocean), not a stated error. Sub-claims: CESM-HR simulates historical MHWs better than CESM-LR and CMIP5 (capability_characterized, §3 ¶6); mean warming explains ≥94% of inclusive-threshold changes (estimate, §4 ¶3); intensity tracks SST variance across LMEs (regularity_in_range, Extended Data Fig. 6); the attribution of the variance increase to ENSO, the IOD and other modes is cited, not tested (best_explanation at most). The P<0.05 test of the LME-group comparison is not described. Supplementary Tables 1-2 were not supplied. No peer-review file was supplied, so no review sequence was coded. Inference: the inherited simulation and the threshold choice predate the analysis, but the paper does not say whether the future-threshold framing was chosen before the results were seen.

disagreements.target: Studies defining future MHWs against a historical (mean warming-inclusive) threshold (refs 9, 15, 17)
disagreements.support: The paper shows that the inclusive threshold yields near-permanent MHWs dominated by mean warming (≥94%, pseudo scenario), whereas the future threshold reveals residual LME-specific increases.
disagreements.quote: there is a built-in increase in MHWs everywhere in the future ocean climate when using a mean [...]

disagreements.target: Low-resolution (~1°) global models, including CMIP5 and CESM-LENS LME projections (refs 17, 20, 27)
disagreements.support: The historical comparison shows larger frequency and intensity biases in CESM-LR and CMIP5 than in CESM-HR, and the coarse models miss the distinct WBC projection changes.
disagreements.quote: ~1° resolution of the global models may not be able to resolve the crucial processes such as ocean eddies and coastal upwelling

disagreements.target: 0.25° satellite SST products (OISST, GMPE) as the benchmark for eddy-scale MHW intensity
disagreements.support: The paper argues from resolution and published high-resolution model results that satellite SST may underestimate variability at 0.1°; it gives no direct test.
disagreements.quote: might lead to underestimation of SST variability at mesoscale-eddy-resolving resolution

disagreements.target: Coarse-resolution projections of WBC regions (CMIP5, CESM-LR)
disagreements.support: CESM-HR projects larger changes and meridional dipoles over the major WBCs that the coarse models do not show.
disagreements.quote: CMIP5 and CESM-LR do not show WBC regions having distinct behaviour relative to other mid-latitude regions
